entries.what_happened: Two manuscripts, both dated 23 September 2026. (1) 'Generalized Cartan-Hadamard isoperimetry and Euclidean equality rigidity' claims that for a complete simply connected smooth Riemannian n-manifold (n >= 2) with sectional curvature at most kappa <= 0, every measurable set E with finite volume and finite ambient perimeter P_g(E) satisfies P_g(E) >= I_{sqrt(-kappa)}(vol(E)), where I_b is the isoperimetric profile of the model space of curvature -b^2 (Theorem 1.1). At kappa = 0 this is P_g(E) >= n omega_n^(1/n) vol(E)^((n-1)/n), equivalently P^n >= n^n omega_n vol^(n-1). It also claims an equality classification at kappa = 0 (Theorem 1.2): for bounded E with 0 < vol(E) < infinity and P_g(E) < infinity, equality in the Euclidean bound holds if and only if E agrees up to null sets with an open region whose induced metric is that of a round Euclidean ball, and the ambient manifold outside that region need not be flat. (2) 'Sharp integral fillings in CAT(0) spaces' claims that every compactly supported integral n-cycle T (n >= 2) in a proper CAT(0) space bounds a compactly supported integral current S with M(S) <= c_n M(T)^((n+1)/n), where c_n = 1/((n+1) s_n^(1/n)) and s_n = area of the unit n-sphere, and that this coefficient is optimal (Theorem 1 of that paper). Its Cartan-Hadamard corollary says that for a Cartan-Hadamard manifold of dimension d >= 3 and a bounded smooth domain Omega, area(boundary of Omega) >= d omega_d^(1/d) vol(Omega)^((d-1)/d). The filling theorem is applied to the integration current of Omega, and top-dimensional constancy gives S = [[Omega]]. The text says the same inequality extends to relatively compact finite-perimeter sets with ambient perimeter, and it handles d = 2 separately by the classical disk inequality (Section 8).
entries.delivers: Part (1) of the problem, the inequality for subsets of a Cartan-Hadamard manifold: manuscript 1 covers every measurable set of finite volume and finite ambient perimeter, with no boundedness, smoothness or connectedness assumption, in every dimension n >= 2. At kappa = 0 this is the Euclidean bound in the form the problem asks. Manuscript 2 covers bounded smooth domains and relatively compact finite-perimeter sets in every dimension d >= 2 (d >= 3 from the filling theorem, d = 2 from the classical disk inequality). Part (2), all dimensions: both manuscripts assert it. Part (3): both manuscripts assert the inequality holds, so the answer to the problem is 'yes'. Part (4), equality: manuscript 1 gives it for bounded sets of positive volume, with equality exactly for a Euclidean ball. Manuscript 2 says nothing about equality. Settlement: manuscript 1 says 'We resolve the generalized Cartan-Hadamard isoperimetric conjecture in every dimension'. Manuscript 2's abstract says 'we prove the Euclidean Cartan-Hadamard isoperimetric conjecture in dimensions at least three', and its body extends this to d = 2. Match to the list: the inequality is the kappa = 0 case of the claims, and the set class is wider than the bullet's smooth-domain reading, as the problem's own note on bounded finite-perimeter sets anticipates. Manuscript 1 also proves a kappa < 0 model comparison that the bullet does not ask for.
entries.remains: If the claims hold, the inequality is covered in every dimension, and the equality case is covered for bounded sets of positive volume. Two gaps remain against problem_asks item (4). Neither manuscript classifies equality for unbounded sets of finite volume, since the rigidity theorem assumes boundedness. Manuscript 2 makes no equality claim at all. Nothing else in the problem is left open by these claims.
entries.direction: proves the conjecture in all dimensions (kappa = 0 case); equality classified for bounded sets
entries.object: No counterexample and no explicit object for the Cartan-Hadamard problem. Euclidean balls are the extremal sets; manuscript 2 (Section 8) checks that the boundary of a Euclidean ball B_R in R^(n+1) attains the filling coefficient. That concerns the filling constant in Euclidean space, not a construction on a Cartan-Hadamard manifold.
entries.conditional_on: Manuscript 1 relies on cited results for the n = 2 and n = 3 cases: the Weil-Bol disk inequality in the Chavel-Feldman form (n = 2) and Kleiner's Theorem 2 (n = 3, cited with page 38). It also uses Gueneysu-Pallara's strict smooth approximation, cited as 'Theorem 2.12 in the author preprint'. Its regularity steps use Ghomi-Spruck Lemma 7.2(i),(ii) for obstacle regularity, Antonelli-Pasqualetto-Pozzetta Corollary 1.6 for almost-minimizer regularity in the equality part, and Brezis-Lieb splitting, with the Aubin-Talenti constant. The hypersurface Sobolev inequality, the confined profile, the n >= 4 comparison, the cutoff passage to infinite volume and the equality rigidity are proved in the paper. Manuscript 2's domain corollary depends on its own integral filling theorem, which is proved by induction on the cycle dimension. That theorem's foundations are Ambrosio-Kirchheim, Wenger, Kirchheim and Sturm's CAT(0) variance inequality, which the text records as standard and cites. The integration-current representation of finite-perimeter sets is cited to Simon 2014, and the d = 2 case is cited to the classical disk inequality (Izmestiev 2014). Manuscript 2 does not depend on manuscript 1.
entries.doubts: Manuscript 2's abstract restricts the Cartan-Hadamard claim to dimensions at least three, but its introduction and Section 8 extend it to every d >= 2 by the classical disk inequality, so the abstract understates the body. Its extension of the domain corollary to finite-perimeter sets is said to follow 'verbatim' from the smooth case, with citations and no separate check. Its foundations theorem (Theorem 'current-background') is recorded from the literature, not proved. Manuscript 1's introduction summarises key steps (the completed square, 'balancing ... forces a first-order identity', the spherical-coordinate variations) in prose, and the full arguments are in the body. In its dimension-two equality argument (Section 8), the periodicity of a boundary component is justified in part by the remark that it 'can also be seen by continuing an oriented arclength chart', with no full proof. Manuscript 1's dimension-three comparison rests entirely on a 1992 citation, not on argument in the paper.
